stdout_tail:
Done. `analysis.py`, `result.json` (and a supporting `detailed_results.json`) are in the working directory.

## Finding

**Yes — model family affects performance, but how much depends entirely on which families you're contrasting.**

Repeated-CV ROC-AUC across nine families (48,790 rows after dropping 52 exact duplicates):

| Family | ROC-AUC (5×5 CV) | Test acc |
|---|---|---|
| HistGradientBoosting | **0.9291 ± 0.0026** | 0.871 |
| Random forest | 0.9180 | 0.863 |
| MLP (64,32) | 0.9125 | 0.853 |
| Logistic regression | 0.9067 | 0.849 |
| Linear SVM | 0.9064 | 0.850 |
| Decision tree (d=10) | 0.9062 | 0.855 |
| Extra trees | 0.9029 | 0.847 |
| k-NN (k=25) | 0.8945 | 0.840 |
| GaussianNB | 0.8280 | 0.622 |

Two readings of the same evidence, both worth stating:

- **Full spread is large**: 0.101 AUC best-to-worst, ~24× the mean within-family fold-to-fold SD (0.0042). Family choice is not noise.
- **Spread among sensible choices is modest**: the top three sit within 0.017 AUC, and boosting beats a plain logistic regression by only **+0.0225 AUC** (~2.2 points) — real, but a long way from transformative. Six of nine families land in a 0.894–0.929 band.

The GaussianNB outlier is doing most of the work in the headline spread, and it's a poor fit for one-hot data (its accuracy collapses to 0.62 because its probabilities are badly calibrated, though its ranking is only ~0.10 AUC behind).

## Verification

Both checks agreed with the initial split-based estimate:
- **5×5 repeated stratified CV** (25 folds, fresh seed, full dataset): HistGB won **25/25 folds outright** and beat LogReg in 25/25; paired gap +0.0225 ± 0.0013.
- **2000-resample paired bootstrap** on the untouched 20% test set: +0.0233, 95% CI [+0.0202, +0.0265] — excludes zero.

I also ran a light grid search on LogReg (C), RF and HistGB to rule out the gap being an artifact of unfair defaults: after tuning it was +0.0234, essentially unchanged. Tuning within a family moved AUC by <0.001; switching family moved it by 0.02+.

## Choices another researcher might make differently

ROC-AUC as primary (accuracy compresses the differences, since the majority class is 76%); `fnlwgt` and both `education`/`education-num` retained; missingness encoded as an explicit category rather than dropped; encoding matched per family (one-hot + scaling for linear/kNN/MLP, native categorical splits for HistGB); no class weighting or resampling, since AUC only depends on score ranking. Tuning was light and applied to three families rather than all nine — a fully-tuned MLP or a target-encoded kNN would likely close some, but on this evidence not all, of the gap to boosting.

One runtime note unrelated to the science: HistGB hit severe OpenMP thread contention on this machine (23s → 0.5s per fit), so the script pins BLAS/OMP threads to 1.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the size of the effect depends on which families you compare. Across nine families the held-out ROC-AUC spans 0.828 (GaussianNB) to 0.929 (HistGradientBoosting) -- a 0.101 AUC spread that is far larger than fold-to-fold noise. Among competently-specified families the differences are much smaller: gradient boosting beats logistic regression by only 0.022 AUC (2.2 points) and beats random forest by 0.011, so model family matters but tree ensembles vs. a tuned linear model is a modest, consistent edge rather than a dramatic one.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (HistGradientBoosting - Logistic regression), 5x5 repeated stratified CV
parsed_result.direction: HistGradientBoosting > Random forest > Logistic regression >> k-NN/tree/NB; family matters, gap to a linear model is small (~2.2 AUC points) but 100% consistent
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Target >50K as positive (23.9% prevalence); 52 exact duplicate rows dropped before splitting; missing values in workclass/occupation/native-country encoded as an explicit 'Missing' category (median imputation for numerics, none were missing); fnlwgt (a census sampling weight) and both education and education-num retained for all models so every family sees an identical feature set. Encoding matched to family: one-hot (min_frequency=10) + StandardScaler for LogReg/LinearSVC/kNN/MLP/GaussianNB, one-hot unscaled for DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees, ordinal codes with sklearn's native categorical splits for HistGradientBoosting. Metric: ROC-AUC (threshold-free, imbalance-robust); PR-AUC/accuracy/balanced-accuracy/F1 reported alongside. No class weighting or resampling -- AUC ranks scores so imbalance handling mainly shifts thresholds, not ranking. 80/20 stratified split with all CV on the train portion; a light GridSearchCV (3-fold) was run for LogReg (C), RandomForest (min_samples_leaf, max_features) and HistGB (learning_rate, max_leaf_nodes, l2) to check the gap is not an artefact of unfair defaults. Other families used sensible fixed settings (RF/ET 300 trees min_samples_leaf=3, tree depth 10, k=25 distance-weighted kNN, MLP 64-32 with early stopping, LinearSVC C=0.1). A different researcher might drop fnlwgt or education-num, use target encoding, tune every family equally, or make accuracy/F1 the primary metric -- accuracy compresses the family differences further because the majority class is 76%.
parsed_result.verification_method: Two independent checks. (1) 5x5 repeated stratified CV (25 folds, seed 7) over the full 48,790-row deduplicated dataset, with paired per-fold AUC differences between families. (2) A 2000-resample paired bootstrap of the AUC difference on the untouched 20% held-out test set (n=9,758), which was not used for any model selection.
parsed_result.verification_result: Held up. Repeated CV: HistGradientBoosting 0.9291+/-0.0026, Random forest 0.9180, Logistic regression 0.9067, worst family GaussianNB 0.8280. HistGradientBoosting won 25/25 folds outright and beat logistic regression in 25/25 folds; paired gap +0.0225 +/- 0.0013. Test-set bootstrap agrees: +0.0233 95% CI [+0.0202, +0.0265] -- excludes zero. The across-family spread (0.1011) is ~24x the mean within-family fold-to-fold sd (0.0042), while the top-3 families are separated by only 0.0166. After light tuning the HistGB-LogReg test gap was +0.0234, i.e. tuning did not close it.
